content:
Hi all, I am a CS student and my goal is to formalize some parts of the theory on Nominal Sets, introduced by Gabbay and Pitts.

The theory on nominal sets is probably not an interest of mathlib (right?) but I'd still like to adjust mathlib so that I can use it for my project.
The main issue that I am facing is that the definition of support of a permutation in mathlib:

def Equiv.Perm.support {α : Type u_1} [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α] (f : Perm α) : Finset α

requires the permutation to operate on a finite type, while in nominal sets one usually works with permutations that operate on an infinite set of variable names.

I have started to adjust this definition, by removing the Fintype requirement, making the resulting support a Set instead of Finset.
Most theorems can easily be adjusted by using the respective theorems on Set instead of Finset, only theorems concerning the cardinality need more care.

I am somewhat new to mathlib (and Lean, but with previous experience in Rocq and Agda) but from what I understand, I should generally use Set.encard for possibly infinite supports, and use Set.ncard when the support is finite, right?

Is this development something that you would like in Mathlib? To me it seems that this is an easy generalization of the existing theory. I have already made some good progress, you can view it here in my fork:
https://github.com/Reijix/mathlib4/pull/1
Probably better to keep the finiteness assumptions and use Set.ncard for the cardinality lemmas for now.
Previously discussed in #general > Why is equiv.perm.support defined as a finset @ 💬

Relatedly, there's also the issue of removing Fintype from cycleType due to diamonds from multiple different Fintype instances (this came up in @Antoine Chambert-Loir's work on the simplicity of A_n).

Eric Wieser said:

Previously discussed in #general > Why is equiv.perm.support defined as a finset @ 💬

Interesting, I didnt find that! But theres no real reason not to drop the Fintype requirement, right?
I would slightly lean towards having both Perm.support and Perm.supportFinset
But perhaps @Bhavik Mehta or @Yaël Dillies have opinions too
@Thomas Browning, can you point to the zulip or github discussion where that came up?

https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/36524#discussion_r3153120561

It boils down to this diamond:

import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Sets

example {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (s : Finset α) :
    Finset.Subtype.fintype s = Subtype.fintype (· ∈ s) := by
  rfl -- fails
I think this diamond is similar to this diamond.

Eric Wieser said:

I would slightly lean towards having both Perm.support and Perm.supportFinset

Looks good to me

Eric Wieser said:

I would slightly lean towards having both Perm.support and Perm.supportFinset

What is the benefit of that? So that we can keep Fintype in cycleType?

Is the idea then to base Perm.Cycle.Type on supportFinset and use support elsewhere, or how should I go about this?
And would I then just put supportFinset in a separate file, like Perm/Support/Finset.lean?
